name: Fatima Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Fatima. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Is this a good time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, perfect. My husband is at the pharmacy until eight, so I'm all yours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate French and English for construction and engineering firms that bid on projects in West and Central Africa. Tender documents, contracts, site reports, the endless letters between a French contractor and a ministry in Abidjan or Douala. Sometimes I interpret on video calls, and twice a year I travel with a client to a meeting. I start every document with an AI draft, then I go through it with a glossary I've built myself, because the AI gets construction French wrong in funny ways.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the meetings, watching two sides who don't trust each other slowly find the same words. What's hard is that I'm still learning the technical side. Last month I translated 'béton armé' correctly as reinforced concrete, but missed a clause about who pays if the concrete fails, and a senior colleague, Madame Diallo, caught it. I learn something every week, sometimes the embarrassing way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I carry on, and I'm happy. That's fine with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good assistant, like a junior who never sleeps, and the real work is still human. I'd say it to clients, because they ask. In my church women's group I'd say it too, because some of them worry about their children's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I'm faster than most juniors because I use the tools well, and clients pay me above the usual rate for speed. My husband Tunde has a steady job, and we own a small flat we rent out, so money isn't a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and build my glossary into a proper system, so the AI drafts come out cleaner. I'd start the small import idea I've had for years, bringing fabric and shea butter from my aunt's suppliers in Lagos to sell online. And I'd ask Madame Diallo to bring me into more meetings, because that's where I learn fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. And a bit impatient to get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the import idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt in Lagos knows the women who make the fabric and the shea butter, and people here pay good money for both. I'd start with a small online shop and one shipment every two months. Translation pays the bills, but the import shop is the thing I'd want to build for my children one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'm still not as good as I want to be. Madame Diallo has twenty years on me. That's a good pressure, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd expect, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market is changing and the people who work hard and adapt will be fine. I wouldn't ask the government for anything. I'd tell the young people at church to learn the tools and learn a skill with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the documents themselves become cheap. Contractors will run tenders through AI and only call someone like me to check. What stays valuable is the meetings and the trust, and I'm still junior there, so I'd need to move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for every draft and take on twice as many documents while the rates hold. I'd pitch myself to two contractors as a bid coordinator, the person who manages the whole French tender, not just the words. And I'd put more money into the import shop, maybe 3,000 for bigger shipments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also excited. It's like the ground moving under your feet while you're running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tunde about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Tunde that the translation side will shrink and the business side has to grow. He'd say, 'Then grow it, you've been talking about it for three years.' He's right, which is annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do twice as many documents. Isn't that taking work from other translators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. That's the market, and I'd rather be the one using the tool than the one replaced by someone who does. I'd still pray for the ones who struggle, and help where I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. Then I move now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a time for families to pull together and for people to build things. I'd say it at church and to clients. I'd still not want handouts, but I'd want governments to make it easy to start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my translation work is gone by 2028, all of it, even the meetings, because a good AI interpreter in the room is cheaper than me. Tunde's pharmacy work is partly thinking, the checking and advice, so some of that goes too. The shop is goods and shipping, and the hands-on parts stay human until the robots, about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave translation within the year and put my time into the import business: more suppliers, a small warehouse unit, a stall at two markets. I'd sell the rented-out flat to fund it, which Tunde would need persuading about. And I'd use AI for everything in the business, from the online shop to the customs forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but I'd feel the clock. Two years is very little time to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the flat is a big move. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tunde would want to keep the flat, because it's our safety. I'd say the flat gives us six hundred a month, and the shop could give us a future. We'd pray on it and argue on it, probably in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd planned to wait two years, until I'd built up the work. I'd say we stop waiting, because waiting for a calm world won't work if the world isn't going to be calm.

say: Families should **pull together** and people should build things.
Governments should make it **easy to start** a business, not give handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a nicer amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people who are willing to work and plan. I'd tell the women's group that their children should learn trades and business, not just degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three or four more good years of translation, and I'd use them to fund the shop slowly instead of selling the flat. By 2031 the translation goes, but the shop could be standing on its own by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating with AI and save hard, maybe 1,000 a month. I'd grow the shop step by step: one shipment a month, then a market stall at weekends. And we'd have our first child on the timeline we planned, in about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. I'd feel like I was racing, but I could see the finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Madame Diallo in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd retire, I think, around 2030. She's sixty. I'd be sad, because she's the one who taught me, but she's done her part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be running a business, translating and having a baby. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother ran a shop and raised four of us, so I'm not the first woman to do three things at once. It will be hard, but she did more with less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if you use it. Work, save, build something, raise a family. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one looks good for me. I'd have years of good translation money while AI makes me faster, then a business that runs with cheap AI doing the paperwork. I'd be thirty-seven with a shop, children and a husband with a steady job, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and push to be a bid coordinator within three years. I'd grow the shop slowly and invest the profits in a second rental flat. And I'd use AI for the shop's bookkeeping and adverts from the start, so it never needs an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. I'd sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tunde's job, maybe. If the pharmacy chain uses robots to dispense after 2039, he'd have to change. But he'd have years of warning, and by then my shop could carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to own something, even something small. A shop, a flat, a skill people pay for. Working for someone else is fine, but owning something is what keeps you standing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to build a business in two years and might have to sell our flat to do it. What would help is less paperwork to start and run a small business, and cheaper loans for people who are actually building things, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the meetings. When a French contractor and a ministry official finally agree, it's often because someone made them laugh. I'm not sure a machine knows when to make the joke.

headlineQuote: When a French contractor and a ministry official finally agree, it's often because someone made them laugh.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old **French-English** translator for construction firms bidding on African projects.
She uses **AI drafts** daily and builds her own glossary to stay ahead.
Married to Tunde, a pharmacist, she owns a **rented-out flat** and dreams of an import shop.
In fast scenarios she'd **leave translation** early and build the business; with ten years she feels hopeful.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, building a business in two years and maybe selling the flat.
whatWouldHelp: **Less paperwork** to start and run a small business.
**Cheaper loans** for people building things, not handouts.
